entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 4 Mi 4:1-13 . Transition to the Glory, Peace, Kingdom, and Victory of Zion. 1-3. Almost identical with Is 2:2-4 . the mountain of the house of the Lord-- which just before ( Mi 3:12 ) had been doomed to be a wild forest height. Under Messiah, its elevation is to be not that of situation, but of moral dignity, as the seat of God's universal empire. people shall flow into it-- In Isaiah it is "all nations": a more universal prophecy.

entries.content_plain: 4. sit every man under his vine, &c.-- that is, enjoy the most prosperous tranquillity ( 1Ki 4:25 ; Zec 3:10 ). The "vine" and "fig tree" are mentioned rather than a house, to signify, there will be no need of a covert; men will be safe even in the fields and open air. Lord of hosts hath spoken it-- Therefore it must come to pass, however unlikely now it may seem.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12759"/><div sID="gen23655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12759"/><hi type="bold">5. For--</hi>rather, Though it be that all people walk after their several gods, yet we (the Jews in the dispersion) will walk in the name of the Lord. So the Hebrew particle means in the Margin, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Ge 8:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.13.17">Ex 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.17.18">Jos 17:18</reference>. The resolution of the exile Jews is: As Jehovah gives us hope of so glorious a restoration, notwithstanding the overthrow of our temple and nation, we must in confident reliance on His promise persevere in the true worship of Him, however the nations around, our superiors now in strength and numbers, walk after their gods [Rosenmuller]. As the Jews were thoroughly weaned from idols by the Babylonian captivity, so they shall be completely cured of unbelief by their present long dispersion (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.8-Zech.10.12">Zec 10:8-12</reference>). <div eID="gen23655" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12762"/><div sID="gen23661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12762"/><hi type="bold">8. tower of the flock--</hi>following up the metaphor of sheep (see on <reference osisRef="Mic.4.6">Mi 4:6</reference>). Jerusalem is called the "tower," from which the King and Shepherd observes and guards His flock: both the spiritual Jerusalem, the Church now whose tower-like elevation is that of doctrine and practice (<reference osisRef="Song.4.4">So 4:4</reference>, "Thy neck is like the tower of David"), and the literal hereafter (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>). In large pastures it was usual to erect a high wooden tower, so as to oversee the flock. Jerome takes the Hebrew for "flock," Eder or Edar, as a proper name, namely, a village near Beth-lehem, for which it is put, Beth-lehem being taken to represent the royal stock of David (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mi 5:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.35.21">Ge 35:21</reference>). But the explanatory words, "the stronghold of the daughter of Zion," confirm English Version.<div eID="gen23661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stronghold--</hi>Hebrew, "Ophel"; an impregnable height on Mount Zion (<reference osisRef="2Chr.27.3">2Ch 27:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.14">33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.26">Ne 3:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen23662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto thee shall ... come ... the first dominion--</hi>namely, the dominion formerly exercised by thee shall come back to thee.<div eID="gen23663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kingdom shall come to the daughter of Jerusalem--</hi>rather, "the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem shall come (again)"; such as it was under David, before its being weakened by the secession of the ten tribes. <div eID="gen23664" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12763"/><div sID="gen23665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12763"/>9. Addressed to the daughter of Zion, in her consternation at the approach of the Chaldeans.<div eID="gen23665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is there no king in thee?--</hi>asked tauntingly. There is a king in her; but it is the same as if there were none, so helpless to devise means of escape are he and his counsellors [Maurer]. Or, Zion's pains are because her king is taken away from her (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.9">Jr 52:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">La 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>) [Calvin]. The former is perhaps the preferable view (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jr 49:7</reference>). The latter, however, describes better Zion's kingless state during her present long dispersion (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen23666" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. Addressed to the daughter of Zion, in her consternation at the approach of the Chaldeans. is there no king in thee?-- asked tauntingly. There is a king in her; but it is the same as if there were none, so helpless to devise means of escape are he and his counsellors [Maurer]. Or, Zion's pains are because her king is taken away from her ( Jr 52:9 ; La 4:20 ; Eze 12:13 ) [Calvin]. The former is perhaps the preferable view (compare Jr 49:7 ). The latter, however, describes better Zion's kingless state during her present long dispersion ( Ho 3:4 , 5 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12764"/><div sID="gen23667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12764"/><hi type="bold">10. Be in pain, and labour--</hi>carrying on the metaphor of a pregnant woman. Thou shalt be affected with bitter sorrows before thy deliverance shall come. I do not forbid thy grieving, but I bring thee consolation. Though God cares for His children, yet they must not expect to be exempt from trouble, but must prepare for it.<div eID="gen23667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go forth out of the city--</hi>on its capture. So "come out" is used <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2Ki 24:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.36.16">Is 36:16</reference>.<div eID="gen23668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwell in the field--</hi>namely, in the open country, defenseless, instead of their fortified city. Beside the Chebar (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.1">Psa 137:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.15">Eze 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Babylon--</hi>Like Isaiah, Micah looks beyond the existing Assyrian dynasty to the Babylonian, and to Judah's captivity under it, and restoration (<reference osisRef="Isa.39.7">Is 39:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.14">43:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">48:20</reference>). Had they been, as rationalists represent, merely sagacious politicians, they would have restricted their prophecies to the sphere of the existing Assyrian dynasty. But their seeing into the far-off future of Babylon's subsequent supremacy, and Judah's connection with her, proves them to be inspired prophets.<div eID="gen23670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there ... there--</hi>emphatic repetition. The very scene of thy calamities is to be the scene of thy deliverance. In the midst of enemies, where all hope seems cut off, there shall Cyrus, the deliverer, appear (compare <reference osisRef="Judg.14.14">Jud 14:14</reference>). Cyrus again being the type of the greater Deliverer, who shall finally restore Israel. <div eID="gen23671" type="x-p"/>

Cyrus again being the type of the greater Deliverer, who shall finally restore Israel.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12765"/><div sID="gen23672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12765"/><hi type="bold">11. many nations--</hi>the subject peoples composing Babylon's armies: and also Edom, Ammon, &c., who exulted in Judah's fall (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">La 2:16</reference>; Ob 11-13).<div eID="gen23672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defiled--</hi>metaphor from a virgin. Let her be defiled (that is, outraged by violence and bloodshed), and let our eye gaze insultingly on her shame and sorrow (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.10">Mi 7:10</reference>). Her foes desired to feast their eyes on her calamities. <div eID="gen23673" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12766"/><div sID="gen23674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12766"/><hi type="bold">12. thoughts of the Lord--</hi>Their unsearchable wisdom, overruling seeming disaster to the final good of His people, is the very ground on which the restoration of Israel hereafter (of which the restoration from Babylon is a type) is based in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.8">Is 55:8</reference>; compare with <reference osisRef="Mic.4.3">Mi 4:3</reference>, 12, 13, which prove that Israel, not merely the Christian Church, is the ultimate subject of the prophecy; also in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.13">Ro 11:13</reference>. God's counsel is to discipline His people for a time with the foe as a scourge; and then to destroy the foe by the hands of His people.<div eID="gen23674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather them as ... sheaves--</hi>them who "gathered" themselves for Zion's destruction (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.11">Mi 4:11</reference>) the Lord "shall gather" for destruction by Zion (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.13">Mi 4:13</reference>), like sheaves gathered to be threshed (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Is 21:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">Jr 51:33</reference>). The Hebrew is singular, "sheaf." However great the numbers of the foe, they are all but as one sheaf ready to be threshed [Calvin]. Threshing was done by treading with the feet: hence the propriety of the image for treading under foot and breaking asunder the foe. <div eID="gen23675" type="x-p"/>

The Hebrew is singular, "sheaf." However great the numbers of the foe, they are all but as one sheaf ready to be threshed [Calvin]. Threshing was done by treading with the feet: hence the propriety of the image for treading under foot and breaking asunder the foe.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12767"/><div sID="gen23676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12767"/><hi type="bold">13. thresh--</hi>destroy thy foes "gathered" by Jehovah as "sheaves" (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.15">Is 41:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen23676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thine horn--</hi>Zion being compared to an ox treading corn, and an ox's strength lying in the horns, her strength is implied by giving her a horn of iron (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.11">1Ki 22:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beat in pieces many--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>).<div eID="gen23678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will consecrate their gain unto the Lord--</hi>God subjects the nations to Zion, not for her own selfish aggrandizement, but for His glory (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.6">Is 60:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.20">Zec 14:20</reference>, with which compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Is 23:18</reference>) and for their ultimate good; therefore He is here called, not merely God of Israel, but "Lord of the whole earth." <chapter eID="Mic.4"/>
